That tiny fact oils a lot of machinery — it is why x² + x + 1 is always odd, why triangular numbers T_n = n(n+1)/2 are integers at all, and it is the first rung of a ladder: products of k consecutive integers are always divisible by k!, a heavyweight theorem whose baby case you just proved.
Why does 12,345,679 × 9 = 111,111,111? And someone showed me × 81 gives all 9s. Coincidence?

Not a coincidence — one identity explains both. Note first that 12,345,679 is 111,111,111 / 9: the famous ‘missing 8’ number (12345679 has no digit 8) is exactly one ninth of the repunit 111,111,111.

Then × 9 trivially gives 111,111,111, and × 81 = × 9 × 9 gives 111,111,111 × 9 = 999,999,999. Both party tricks are the same fact at different volumes.

Where does 1/9 come in? The decimal expansion of 1/81 is 0.012345679012345679... — the digits 0 through 9 in order, with 8 swallowed by a carry (the true pattern is ...012345679..., the 8 absorbed where 9 + 1 rolls over). Multiply 1/81 by 10^9-ish scaling and you meet 12,345,679 again. So the number is a fossil of the fraction 1/81: a repeating decimal whose period almost counts for you, ruined — or perfected — by one carry.

Most ‘magic numbers’ in recreational arithmetic are like this: a rational number’s decimal period, photographed at the right magnification.
Consecutive squares: 50² = 2,500 and 51² = 2,601. The gap is 101. Is there a pattern to these gaps I can exploit?

The gaps are the odd numbers, in order. (n + 1)² − n² = 2n + 1 — expand the left side and the n² terms cancel, leaving exactly the (n+1)-th odd number. Between 50² and 51²: 2 × 50 + 1 = 101. Between 51² and 52²: 103, giving 52² = 2,601 + 103 = 2,704.

Exploit it as a computation ladder: if you know one square, you can walk to neighbors by adding or subtracting consecutive odds. From 60² = 3,600, get 59² by subtracting 2 × 60 − 1 = 119: 3,600 − 119 = 3,481. Correct — 59² = 3,481.

And the pattern is the sum-of-odds theorem read backwards: if consecutive squares differ by the odd numbers, then summing the first n odd numbers must rebuild n² from 0², which is the L-shaped tile picture from the other direction. Two views of one identity: differences of squares are odds; sums of odds are squares. A great deal of mathematics is learning to read an equation in both directions.
Take a two-digit number, reverse it, subtract the smaller from the larger. 52 − 25 = 27, 83 − 38 = 45, 61 − 16 = 45... the answer is always a multiple of 9. Why?

Write the number as 10a + b, with a the tens digit and b the units. Reversed, it is 10b + a. Subtract: (10a + b) − (10b + a) = 9a − 9b = 9(a − b). A multiple of 9, always, and in fact the multiple is exactly 9 times the difference of the digits. Your examples: 52 has digit difference 3, giving 27. 83 and 61 both have digit difference 5, giving 45.

The deeper statement: a number and any rearrangement of its digits are congruent mod 9, because both are congruent to the digit sum. So their difference is divisible by 9. Reversal is just the two-digit rearrangement.

This is also the skeleton of a classic mind-reading trick: have someone do the reversal subtraction secretly, then tell you all but one digit of the result. The result is a multiple of 9, its digits must sum to 9 or 18, and the missing digit is forced. The trick is casting out nines in a magician’s hat.
What is Kaprekar’s constant? Start me at 3524 and show me the machine running.

The machine: take a 4-digit number, arrange its digits descending and ascending, subtract the smaller from the larger, repeat. Kaprekar’s constant, 6174, is where every valid input ends up.

Run 3524. Digits sorted: 5432 and 2345. Subtract: 5432 − 2345 = 3,087. Next round: 8730 − 0378 = 8,352. Next: 8532 − 2358 = 6,174. Arrived in three steps. And 6174 is a genuine fixed point: 7641 − 1467 = 6,174, so the machine parks there forever.

The fine print: inputs with all four digits equal (1111, 7777) collapse to 0000 instead — the one degenerate case. Every other 4-digit number reaches 6174 in at most 7 rounds. There is a 3-digit sibling, 495, with the same property.

Why it works is subtler than that it works — the subtraction forces the digits into a shrinking family of patterns (every result after the first step is a multiple of 9, another mod-9 fingerprint, since the descending and ascending arrangements share a digit sum), and 6174 is the unique survivor. Kaprekar was a schoolteacher in India who found this in 1949 with pencil and patience; it remains the friendliest example of an attractor in all of recreational mathematics.
Prove there are infinitely many primes. The real Euclid proof, please, not a hand-wave.

Euclid’s proof, by contradiction. Suppose there were only finitely many primes: p₁, p₂, ..., p_n, the complete list. Form the number N = (p₁ × p₂ × ... × p_n) + 1 — multiply them all, then add one.

Now, N is greater than 1, so it has at least one prime divisor; call it q. (Every integer above 1 has a prime divisor: take its smallest divisor above 1, which must be prime.) Ask whether q is on the list. If q = p_i for some i, then q divides the product p₁...p_n, and q also divides N — so q divides their difference, N minus the product, which is 1. But no prime divides 1. Contradiction. Therefore q is a prime not on the list — the list was not complete.

Since any finite list of primes can be extended this way, no finite list contains all of them: the primes are infinite.

Notice the proof’s exact shape, because it is often misquoted: it does not say N itself is prime (often it is not). It says N’s prime factors are all new. That distinction is the difference between a proof and a fallacy, and it is 2,300 years old.
In Euclid’s proof you multiply the first primes and add 1. For 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13 that gives some number — is that number itself prime?

Compute it: 2 × 3 × 5 × 7 × 11 × 13 = 30,030, so N = 30,031. And no — 30,031 = 59 × 509, composite.

This is exactly the subtlety that separates Euclid’s proof from its popular retelling. The proof never claims N is prime. It claims N has a prime factor outside the starting list — and here that is gloriously visible: 59 and 509 are both primes, both bigger than 13, both absent from {2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13}. The construction delivered two new primes while itself being composite.

Why must the factors be new? Any prime on the list divides 30,030 exactly, so it leaves remainder 1 on dividing 30,031 — it cannot divide N. Hence every prime factor of N is a discovery.

Smaller cases flatter the construction: 2×3 + 1 = 7, 2×3×5 + 1 = 31, 2×3×5×7 + 1 = 211, 2×3×5×7×11 + 1 = 2,311 — all prime, which seduces people into the false pattern. 30,031 is the first failure, and it fails in the instructive direction: the theorem survives precisely because it promised less than the pattern suggested.
What makes 6 and 28 ‘perfect’ numbers?

A perfect number equals the sum of its proper divisors — all its divisors except itself. For 6, the proper divisors are 1, 2, 3, and 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. Perfect balance. For 28: 1, 2, 4, 7, 14, summing to 1 + 2 + 4 + 7 + 14 = 28.

Most numbers miss. Deficient numbers fall short (8: 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 < 8; every prime is deeply deficient, summing to just 1). Abundant numbers overshoot (12: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 6 = 16 > 12). Perfection is the knife’s edge between them, and it is rare: the sequence begins 6, 28, 496, 8,128, and then leaps to 33,550,336.

The ancients knew the first four and draped them in mysticism; the modern view is colder and better — perfection turns out to be welded to Mersenne primes, one perfect number per Mersenne prime, by a theorem of Euclid completed by Euler. Rare arithmetic, exact structure: the mystics were wrong about the meaning but right about the specialness.
Where do 496 and 8,128 come from? Is there a formula for even perfect numbers?

There is, and it is one of the oldest formulas in mathematics. Euclid showed: if 2^p − 1 is prime (a Mersenne prime), then 2^(p−1) × (2^p − 1) is perfect. Euler proved the converse two thousand years later: every even perfect number has exactly this form.

Run it. p = 5: 2^5 − 1 = 31, prime, so the perfect number is 2^4 × 31 = 16 × 31 = 496. p = 7: 2^7 − 1 = 127, prime, giving 2^6 × 127 = 64 × 127 = 8,128. The earlier ones: p = 2 gives 2 × 3 = 6; p = 3 gives 4 × 7 = 28.

Why does the formula work? The divisors of 2^(p−1) × q (with q = 2^p − 1 prime) can be listed in two rows — powers of 2, and those same powers times q — and their sum telescopes to exactly twice the number, which is perfection restated. The failed exponent p = 11 (where 2^11 − 1 = 23 × 89 is composite) correspondingly produces no perfect number.

So the census of even perfect numbers is exactly the census of Mersenne primes: 52 known, the largest built from the 2024 record prime. The formula is complete for even numbers — and silent about odd ones.
Does an odd perfect number exist?

Nobody knows — it is one of the oldest open problems in mathematics, open since antiquity in spirit and untouched in essence.

What is known is a portrait of the fugitive, assembled from necessary conditions. An odd perfect number, if it exists, must exceed 10^1500 (a proven lower bound — the search has been pushed that far by structured argument, not brute force). It must have at least 10 distinct prime factors, at least 75 prime factors counted with multiplicity, a largest prime factor above 10^60, and a specific restricted shape (Euler showed it must be a prime power times a square, with the prime ≡ 1 mod 4). Condition by condition, the hypothetical number is being described to death without being found.

Most number theorists suspect it does not exist, and some have argued the constraints are close to contradictory — but ‘close’ has been the status for decades. Meanwhile the even side is fully solved by the Euclid–Euler theorem. It is a strange landscape: half the problem finished in the 1700s, the other half not finished at all. If you want a problem to test a new idea on, this one has been waiting two millennia.
What are amicable numbers? Show me the smallest pair actually working.

Two numbers are amicable if each equals the sum of the other’s proper divisors — perfect numbers are the lonely case where a number is its own partner. The smallest pair is 220 and 284, known since antiquity.

Proper divisors of 220: 1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 11, 20, 22, 44, 55, 110. Sum: 1 + 2 + 4 + 5 + 10 + 11 + 20 + 22 + 44 + 55 + 110 = 284. Proper divisors of 284: 1, 2, 4, 71, 142. Sum: 1 + 2 + 4 + 71 + 142 = 220. Each generates the other — the books balance in both directions.

The pair was a talisman for centuries (friendship charms, literally), and a formula attributed to Thābit ibn Qurra in the 9th century generates some pairs from special primes. But amicable numbers resist complete understanding: over a billion pairs are now known by computer search, yet it is still unproved whether infinitely many pairs exist, and unknown whether a pair can have opposite parity... in fact every known pair shares parity, and whether a mixed pair exists is open too. Even the friendly numbers keep secrets.
220 and 284 were found in antiquity. When was the second amicable pair discovered, and by whom?

Not until 1866 — and by a 16-year-old Italian schoolboy, Niccolò Paganini (no relation to the violinist). The pair is 1184 and 1210.

Verify it the way he had to, by hand. Proper divisors of 1184: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 37, 74, 148, 296, 592. Sum: 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 + 32 = 63; then 63 + 37 + 74 + 148 + 296 + 592 = 1,210. Proper divisors of 1210: 1, 2, 5, 10, 11, 22, 55, 110, 121, 242, 605. Sum: 1 + 2 + 5 + 10 + 11 + 22 + 55 + 110 + 121 + 242 + 605 = 1,184. The pair balances.

The astonishing part is the gap: the pair sat undiscovered for roughly two thousand years while Fermat, Descartes, and Euler all worked on amicable numbers and found other pairs (Fermat’s 17,296 and 18,416, for instance) — all much larger. Paganini’s pair is the second smallest there is. Generations of masters, armed with generating formulas, walked past a small pair that a teenager found by direct divisor-summing. It remains the standing advertisement for brute force honestly applied: formulas find what they are shaped to find, and sometimes the treasure is just below the search pattern.
Walk me through the Collatz sequence for 27. I hear it is weirdly dramatic for such a small number.
What is the actual status of the Collatz conjecture? Proven for small numbers, believed, doubted — where does it stand?

The conjecture: starting from any positive integer, the rule ‘halve if even, triple and add 1 if odd’ eventually reaches 1. Status: unproved, despite being checkable by a child and attacked for nearly ninety years.

The evidence is enormous. Computers have verified that every starting number up to beyond 10^20 eventually reaches 1 — no counterexample can be small. There are also real theorems in the neighborhood: Terence Tao proved in 2019 that ‘almost all’ starting values eventually get down to a tiny fraction of their size (a precise statement about density), the strongest result of its kind.

Why does proof resist? The odd step multiplies by roughly 3 while the even step divides by 2, and on average the drift is downward — heuristically each odd excursion is followed by enough halvings to shrink by a factor of about 3/4 per odd step. But ‘on average’ is not ‘always’: a proof must rule out both a cycle hiding at large height and a trajectory that escapes to infinity, and the process is chaotic enough that local analysis keeps failing to globalize. Paul Erdős reportedly said mathematics is not yet ready for such problems.

So the honest summary: verified to 10^20, believed by essentially everyone, proved by no one. Collatz is the purest example that a statement’s difficulty has almost nothing to do with the difficulty of stating it.
Twin primes are unproved, but I recall some breakthrough about prime gaps in 2013. What exactly was proved?

In 2013, Yitang Zhang — then a little-known lecturer — proved that there are infinitely many pairs of primes separated by at most 70,000,000. It sounds like a weak shadow of twin primes (gap 2), and numerically it is. Conceptually it was a landslide: before Zhang, no one could prove that any bounded gap, however huge, recurs infinitely often. The primes might, as far as anyone knew, have drifted apart forever; Zhang proved they cannot — some fixed gap repeats endlessly.

Then the number collapsed. Through the collaborative Polymath project and a key improvement by James Maynard (independently also developed by Tao), the bound was driven from 70,000,000 down to 246: there are infinitely many prime pairs at distance at most 246.

The remaining distance from 246 to 2 is not a matter of more of the same effort — the methods are believed to stall well above 2 (the ‘parity barrier’), and closing the gap needs a genuinely new idea. So the current map reads: bounded gaps, proved; gap exactly 2, conjectured; and the frontier sits at 246, waiting. It is the modern shape of progress on ancient problems — not a single leap to the summit, but the mountain’s height being measured, publicly, year by year.
Are there infinitely many primes that are 3 mod 4 — like 3, 7, 11, 19, 23? Or could they run out?

They cannot run out, and this case has an Euclid-style proof you can follow. Suppose there were only finitely many such primes, q₁, ..., q_k. Build N = 4 × (q₁ × ... × q_k) − 1.

N ≡ −1 ≡ 3 (mod 4). Now the key lemma: a product of numbers each ≡ 1 (mod 4) is ≡ 1 (mod 4), so N — which is ≡ 3 (mod 4) — cannot have all its prime factors ≡ 1 (mod 4). At least one prime factor p of N satisfies p ≡ 3 (mod 4). Is p on the list? Every listed q_i divides 4 × (q₁...q_k), so if p were one of them, p would divide N and N + 1’s sibling quantity — precisely, p would divide the difference, which works out to 1. Impossible. So p is a new prime ≡ 3 (mod 4), contradicting the list’s completeness.

The general statement is Dirichlet’s theorem (1837): for any coprime a and d, the progression a, a + d, a + 2d, ... contains infinitely many primes. The 3-mod-4 case is one of only a few with an elementary proof; Dirichlet’s full theorem needed him to invent analytic number theory to prove it. Some infinitudes are one clever construction deep; others are one new field deep.
I heard Euler proved there are infinitely many primes using a sum that diverges. How can a sum prove that?

Consider the sum of reciprocals of the primes: 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/5 + 1/7 + 1/11 + ... Euler showed this sum diverges — it grows without bound, like the harmonic series and unlike, say, the sum of 1/n² over all n, which converges.

Now suppose there were only finitely many primes. Then every integer’s reciprocal could be built from those finitely many primes’ reciprocals through the geometric-series identity behind the Euler product: the harmonic sum would equal a finite product of finite quantities — it would have to converge. But the harmonic series diverges. Contradiction; hence infinitely many primes. Euler’s sharper finding, that the prime reciprocal sum itself diverges, says more: the primes are ‘dense enough’ that their reciprocals still pile up to infinity, even though their density tends to zero. Compare the squares: 1/n² sums to a finite total, so squares are, in this precise sense, rarer than primes.

This proof matters beyond its conclusion. It founded analytic number theory — the idea that questions about whole numbers can be settled by the behavior of infinite sums and products — and its descendant, the Riemann zeta function, sits under the prime number theorem and the most famous open problem in mathematics. A divergence argument from 1737 is still load-bearing.
Every few years there’s a headline about a new largest prime. Why does this keep happening — shouldn’t we run out of headlines?

Euclid guarantees the supply: there is no largest prime, so there is always a bigger one to find, and the record is limited only by our ability to test candidates. The headlines recur because the ability keeps improving on three fronts at once.

Hardware: the 2024 record prime, 2^136,279,841 − 1, was found with GPUs — the first record set that way — and distributed projects like GIMPS aggregate thousands of volunteers’ machines into a single search instrument. Algorithms: the Lucas–Lehmer test for Mersenne numbers keeps getting faster implementations. And motivation: there are modest cash prizes for record primes, plus the institutional glory of a discovery with your name on it, plus the fact that each new Mersenne prime automatically mints a new largest known perfect number.

The honest caveat for headline-readers: ‘largest known prime’ is a statement about search, not about the primes themselves. The record holder is not the most important prime, just the most remote one currently reachable — always a Mersenne prime, because that is where the fast tests live. The headlines will keep coming at the pace of computing, and each one is really a story about us, not about the numbers: the frontier moved because the machines did.
What does the prime number theorem actually say, in numbers I can check?

It says the count of primes up to x, written π(x), is approximately x / ln x — and the approximation’s relative error shrinks toward zero as x grows.

Check it small, where you can count exactly. π(100) = 25. The theorem’s estimate: 100 / ln 100 = 100 / 4.605 ≈ 21.7. Error: about 13% low. π(1000) = 168. Estimate: 1000 / ln 1000 = 1000 / 6.908 ≈ 144.8. Error: about 14% low. At these heights the relative error is barely improving, which is honest reporting about the theorem: it is an asymptotic statement, and its convergence is famously slow and uneven; a refined estimate using the logarithmic integral li(x) does far better even here (li(1000) ≈ 178, within about 6%).

What the theorem really delivers is the shape of the prime world: density 1/ln x near x, average gaps of ln x, and the certainty that primes thin out logarithmically — never exponentially, never to nothing. Proved in 1896 by Hadamard and de la Vallée Poussin (independently, using the zeta function), it converted three centuries of numerical pattern-spotting into knowledge. The gap between the estimate 144.8 and the truth 168 at x = 1000 is not a failure of the theorem; it is a reminder that ‘eventually accurate’ and ‘accurate by Tuesday’ are different promises.
Final boss: Marin Mersenne listed 2^67 − 1 among his primes. Was he right?

He was wrong, and the correction is one of the great scenes in mathematics. 2^67 − 1 = 147,573,952,589,676,412,927 — and it factors: 147,573,952,589,676,412,927 = 193,707,721 × 761,838,257,287.

The story, as it is usually told: in 1903, the mathematician Frank Nelson Cole presented at an American Mathematical Society meeting. Without saying a word, he computed 2^67 on one blackboard, then multiplied 193,707,721 by 761,838,257,287 on another — digit by digit, in silence — until the two results stood identical. He sat down to a standing ovation. Asked later how long the factorization had taken him, he reportedly said: ‘three years of Sundays.’

Mersenne’s list (1644) had stood for over 250 years with 67 wrongly included (and a couple of correct entries, like 2^61 − 1, needing separate proof). The moral ties the whole subject together: a prime exponent is necessary for a Mersenne prime but never sufficient — 2^11 − 1 fails small, 2^67 − 1 fails at the edge of hand computation — and authority is not evidence. Cole’s Sundays are the rebuttal: in number theory, the check is the truth, and the check is available to anyone willing to do the arithmetic.
